title: Welcoming birth
hookLine: the other end of life: traditions welcome birth

cards: A hospital corridor at three in the morning, or a bedroom at home, or a car that didn't make it in time. A small, furious, astonished person has just arrived, and the room changes.
This stretch of the path has been about the end of life: rites for the dying, words for the grieving, letters for after. It would be lopsided to leave out the other end.
The traditions that mourn the dead also have ways of greeting the newborn. Today: three welcomes, from three homes.

teach.b: First, a waiting man holds a baby.

In Luke's Gospel, Mary and Joseph bring the infant Jesus to the Temple, and a man named Simeon, who has been told he won't see death before he sees the Lord's Christ, takes him: "Then took he him up in his arms, and blessed God."
His song begins with his own death: "Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace." At the very start of one life, another man says he's ready to go. Birth and death, in one pair of arms.

teach.h: A CALL WHISPERED IN THE EAR.
teach.b: Second, a call whispered in the ear.
In Muslim tradition, the call to prayer, the adhan, may be softly spoken into a newborn's right ear, so that among the first words the child hears are the words that call people to prayer.
Some hadith collections report the Prophet ﷺ doing this for his grandson.

teach.h: A NAME FROM AN OPEN PAGE.
teach.b: Third, a name from an open page. In a Sikh naming ceremony, the family gathers before the Guru Granth Sahib, the scripture is opened, and a passage is read.
Its first letter guides the first letter of the child's name, so the scripture, in a sense, joins in the naming.

Christian families may baptize or dedicate a child, Jewish families may hold a naming or a brit, Hindu families have their own rites for name and first food, and Buddhist families may bring a baby for blessing.
Each has its own meaning, kept in its own home. What they share is simple: a new person is not just born, but received.

how: Muslim families may whisper the adhan in a newborn's right ear; Sikh families name a child from a passage of the Guru Granth Sahib; Christian families may baptize or dedicate children, and Jewish families may hold a naming or a brit.

games.q: you're Simeon, led by the Spirit into the Temple. a couple carries in their baby. what do you do?
o: you watch them pass and say nothing.
you take the baby up in your arms and bless God.
you ask them to come back another day.
games.why: Simeon takes him up in his arms, blesses God, and sings that he can now depart in peace.

practice: Think of someone new in your life, or about to be, a baby among family or friends, a new neighbor, a new colleague, a child just starting school, and hold them in mind for a few breaths.
Let a sense of welcome gather, the way it might if you were holding them. If you pray, you can bless them in the words of your own tradition.
